Parshas Bereishis

Knowing Our Worth, Embracing Our Words

Ascent from the Chagim

As we open Parshas Bereishis, we aren't simply reading about the beginning of the world — we are experiencing a renewal of reality itself. But we do so as people who have just emerged from the intense spiritual journey of Tishrei. We've crowned Hashem as King on Rosh Hashanah, purified ourselves on Yom Kippur, and basked in closeness and joy through Sukkos and Simchas Torah. So what now? How do we carry that spiritual energy forward into the year? The answer lies not only in the newness of the world, but in the role we play in that renewed world.

From Surrender to Strength

In Sefer Devarim, we saw the continuing theme of bitul — of nullification of my animalistic will before the will of Hashem, and of an individual learning how they are needed and able to contribute to the whole and the greater good. But before we can surrender to the will of Hashem, we must first believe in the value of the self. Otherwise, what is it that we are surrendering? As we restart the Torah with Parshas Bereishis, a shift occurs. We are reintroduced to ourselves not as just parts of a whole, but as active partners in creation, each and every one of us having this focus and ability.

Hashem says, "Na'aseh adam b'tzalmeinu" — "Let us make man in Our image" (Bereishis 1:26). Rashi, quoting the Midrash (Bereishis Rabbah 8:7), explains that Hashem consulted His heavenly court. The act of creation was not unilateral. It was collaborative on one level, but not in essence — because when the Torah describes the actual creation of Adam, it says: "Vayivra Elokim et ha'adam b'tzalmo" — "And G-d created man in His image" (Bereishis 1:27). Not in their image. Not in the image of the angels. In Hashem's image. And that's the key: we are not mishutafim because we were created by consensus, we are mishutafim because we were created in His image. And His ratzon, as proven by our very existence, is to create. That tzelem Elokim is what empowers us to create, to choose, to speak, to shape, and to elevate. It's not an invitation to arrogance, but a call to responsibility.

The Koach of Speech

The most striking way that man reflects the Divine is in the power of speech. Hashem creates the world through speech. "Vayomer Elokim yehi or" — "And G-d said: Let there be light" (Bereishis 1:3). Adam too is granted the power of words. He names each creature in Gan Eden, not arbitrarily, but with insight. The name he gives reflects the inner reality of that being. But that power can be distorted. When Chava is persuaded by the nachash to eat from the Eitz HaDaas, she alters Hashem's words ever so slightly. And Adam, instead of taking responsibility, uses his words to shift blame: "The woman whom You gave me, she gave me from the tree." Chava then deflects as well: "The serpent deceived me." From the beginning, we see the immense weight that words carry. They can name and words can create. But they can also mislead and avoid.

Had Adam used his power of speech to do Viduy, confession, when Hashem asked him where he was and what he had done, perhaps Hashem would have accepted this teshuvah and would have never sent Adam and Chava out of Eden to begin with — as we are taught that teshuvah existed before the world was created.

Created for Me, but Not First

The Gemara in Sanhedrin (37a) teaches that each person must say: "Bishvili nivra ha'olam" — "The world was created for me." The human being was created last, not because he is least important, but because he is the purpose of creation. Yet the very next page (Sanhedrin 38a) offers a critical counterbalance: "If he becomes haughty, he is told: The mosquito preceded you in creation." We are at once the center of the banquet and the last guest to arrive. The universe was prepared for us, but we must enter with humility. This duality is not a contradiction — it is the posture of a Jew. To carry greatness without arrogance. To bear responsibility without self-importance.

The Moon and Its Message

This balance finds profound expression in the story of the moon. Rashi (Bereishis 1:16) brings the Midrash (Chullin 60b): at first, the sun and moon were equal. But the moon protested: "Two kings cannot wear one crown." Hashem responded: "Go and diminish yourself." The moon was made smaller, its light reflective rather than original. But Hashem consoled the moon. The Jewish people would be linked to it. They would count their months by its phases. Righteous people would be compared to it. The moon's power is not in its brightness, but in its timing, its cycles, and its constancy. It pulls the tides, influences the core of the earth, and governs the rhythm of time itself. And yet, it does so humbly, in the background, through borrowed light. The Jewish people are like the moon. Sometimes full, sometimes diminished. Sometimes celebrated, sometimes forgotten. But we are always necessary.

A Final Charge

The world today feels uncertain. We have experienced loss, fear, and confusion. But the Torah tells us: you matter. Your words, your presence, your actions all have the power of creation from Hashem and they can change things. So as we began — and to remind ourselves again: before we can fully surrender to the will of Hashem, we must first believe in the value of the self, our ability to grant comfort, to change the world, to heal others, and to create. Parshas Bereishis is a time of renewal — a time to take on new commitments, to set goals, to speak words of love and blessing, to build, not destroy, to reflect light, even if it is borrowed light, for that too is divine. May we merit to rise and shine again, until the time of Mashiach, when the moon and the sun will once again shine with equal strength, and the light of every Jew will be seen in its full glory. Shabbat Shalom.

Parshas Noach

Tafkid, Messaging, and Identity

This week's challenge wasn't in finding Torah to speak about — quite the opposite. There was too much to say. So many ideas, but the delivery felt stuck. And maybe that's exactly the point: the how of the message depends deeply on the who that is delivering it. Every message must come through the prism of the self. And that's why this parsha strikes such a chord.

Noach's Individual Tafkid

Noach is called a tzaddik in his generation (Bereishis 6:9). He walked with Hashem. That's not a side note — it's a profound identity. But he didn't do outreach like Avraham. He built the teivah, saved his family, and followed Hashem's word precisely. That was his avodah. We often focus on what he didn't do — but what he did do requires enormous strength. Noach lived in a time of total corruption (Bereishis 6:11). In such a time, Noach's righteousness was not a passive quality. It was built through boundaries. He created space between himself and the outside. He didn't absorb the world; he protected his teivah. When people asked him what he was building, he told them and he told them why. He wasn't silent, he didn't compromise, and he didn't lower the message. He just didn't go out to find people — he told them when they came to him.

The Raven and the Dove

When it came time to re-engage the world, Noach sent out the raven first (Bereishis 8:7). The raven didn't fulfill the mission. Rashi explains that the raven was suspicious that Noach had ulterior motives. But the Gemara in Pesachim 113b hints to us something else: ravens are among those species that love their own kind. The raven may not have succeeded, but it is a creature of connection and loyalty. Later, ravens find their moment. In the days of Eliyahu HaNavi, it is the raven that feeds him (Melachim I 17:4-6). In the right context, its koach became invaluable. The dove, on the other hand, fulfills its task (Bereishis 8:11). It flies out, returns with the olive branch. Doves are quiet, personal birds. And later, we see doves brought as korbanos — for the poor, the recovering mother, the baal teshuvah. They are korbanos of individuals. The raven and the dove represent two modes of mission. Each is holy in its time.

From Noach to Avraham: A Generational Shift

After the mabul, the world rebuilds. But then we see the Tower of Bavel — a massive collective project, but without proper spiritual grounding (Bereishis 11:4). Mass cooperation aimed in the wrong direction. At this point, Avram arises. His koach is outreach. He teaches and spreads the name of Hashem (Bereishis 12:5; Rashi). This is a different tafkid than Noach's — and it is needed now. Yet Noach and Avram overlapped for 57 years (Seder Olam Rabbah ch. 1). The transition was not immediate. Both roles coexisted. Sometimes the world needs a Noach. Sometimes an Avram. And sometimes both.

Water: Destruction or Nurture

The mabul water was boiling and acidic. But we also say ein mayim ela Torah (Bava Kamma 17a). Water can destroy, or it can nurture. The same substance, depending on direction. The Mabul began on the 17th of Mar Cheshvan (Rashi, Bereishis 7:11). In Eretz Yisrael, we begin davening for rain on the 7th — ten days earlier. An opportunity of ten days of preparation, of bracha-seeking before the memory of destruction. We are reminded: water is coming. Will it be a mabul or a mikvah?

Final Reflections

We are not Noach. We are not Avraham. But we carry something from both. There are times we need to retreat and preserve. There are times we need to step out and speak. The key is to discern which tafkid is ours today. And to never forget that even within what looks like inaction, there may be deep avodah taking place. May we be zocheh to recognize our individual tafkid, to honor the different voices within our mesorah, and to draw down water that heals and nourishes, not water that floods and burns. Gut Shabbos.

Parshas Lech Lecha

The Beginnings of Z'chut Avot

A Turning Point in Torah

This week's parsha marks a turning point in the Torah's story. Until now, Bereishis has been about humanity. With Lech Lecha, Hashem turns His attention to one man, and through Avram, the story of the Avos begins which eventually leads to us.

The Meaning of Z'chus Avos

We often speak about z'chus Avos — the merit of our forefathers — as if it is something automatically inherited, a spiritual trust fund that protects us through life. But z'chus Avos is not just an unearned reward. It is a connection. It means we have access to the same inner strength, the same faith, the same courage that they lived by. To benefit from their z'chus, we must also continue their path.

The Command to Go

When Hashem tells him, Lech lecha mei'artzecha — leave your land, your birthplace, your father's house — Avram had already left Ur Kasdim and was in Charan. So why tell him to go again? Chazal explain that this was not about distance, but about depth. 'Go for yourself,' says Hashem — not to escape the past, but to uncover your essence. Growth is never just about leaving; it is about becoming. From that moment, Avram's life becomes a series of journeys, each one testing his faith and refining his soul. Each time, he moves forward, not backward. Each time, he discovers a new dimension of emunah — a faith that does not depend on comfort or certainty.

The Fear in Egypt: Seeing the Best in Others

One puzzling moment stands out: when Avram tells Sarai to say she is his sister. How could the man who survived being put into a fiery furnace fear for his life? The mefarshim explain that Avram did not doubt Hashem's power — he doubted his worthiness. Perhaps he thought he had already used up his miracles. There is a deeper beauty here. The Midrash says that just as Avram trusted that Sarai would be saved through her own righteousness, Sarai trusted that Avram would be saved through his. Each believed in the other more than in themselves. The Lubavitcher Rebbe taught that people often look at others with the right eye — with kindness — and at themselves with the left eye, with stringency. But we can learn to look at ourselves and others with both eyes in a fair and balanced way.

Beyond the Stars

When Hashem took Avram 'outside,' showing him the stars and saying, 'Look toward the heavens… so shall your children be,' He was teaching him that faith itself must rise above nature. Avram could not have children according to the stars, so Hashem lifted him beyond them. He didn't just change Avram's fate; He changed the very definition of faith. Avram had the courage to follow through with his emunah in Hashem and His promises, to change himself so that he would be continuously going out to himself and out to others together. In our earliest stages, we can already start to change who we are, what our reality is, what our direction and purpose are. And then as we, their legacy, live forward this way, we get to tap into z'chus avos.

Our Living Legacy

Avram and Sarai began as a couple who could not have children. Yet today, we — their descendants — are the proof of what faith can create. We are their living legacy, the continuation of that moment when Hashem said, 'Look up.' As we enter Shabbos Lech Lecha, we can all hear that same call: Lech lecha — go forward. Step out of what's familiar. Not because we're unworthy, but because we are worthy of growing further. Like Avram, we too are invited to move beyond the limits of nature, beyond the stories we tell ourselves, and to walk toward the person Hashem knows we can become.

Parshas Vayeira

Mesirat Nefesh and Chazakas

Parshas Vayeira has a fascinating theme that runs not only through the parsha itself, but echoes throughout Tanach and even Halacha: the power and pattern of the number three. The number three carries weight, structure, and meaning.

The Pattern of Three in Torah and Halacha

Across Jewish tradition, we find foundational groupings of three: The 6,000 years of the world are divided into three periods — 2,000 years of tohu (chaos), 2,000 years of Torah, and 2,000 years connected to Mashiach. In Halacha, a chazakah (presumption of permanence) is established after three consistent occurrences. A Beis Din requires three members. A young boy's chinuch formally begins at age three, marked by the upsherin in many communities. In this week's parsha, Avraham is visited by three angels as he recovers from his bris milah; Sarah is asked to prepare three se'ah of flour for bread; and Avraham selects three calves to serve his guests, one for each angel.

The Threefold Command of the Akeidah

One of the most profound uses of the number three appears in the command Hashem gives to Avraham regarding the Akeidah: 'Kach na es bincha, es yechidcha, asher ahavta, es Yitzchak' — Please take your son, your only one, whom you love, Yitzchak. Chazal explain, further elaborated by Rashi, that Hashem didn't need to go through this list for Avraham's sake — he would have fulfilled a single command without hesitation. It was done this way to teach the levels of growth and z'chut for each level. The Sfas Emes elaborates that the progression is for us, the descendants of Avraham. Each stage represents an increasing level of emotional and spiritual difficulty: Bincha — your son; Yechidcha — your only one; Asher Ahavta — whom you love. Avraham is being asked to give not just a child, but everything: his love, his legacy, his nation's destiny. And yet, he walks forward.

Mesiras Nefesh and the Three Cardinal Sins

The Gemara in Sanhedrin 74a teaches that there are three aveiros for which a Jew must give up their life rather than transgress: Avodah Zarah (idolatry), Giluy Arayos (forbidden relationships), and Shefichas Damim (murder). Each of these corresponds with a layer of the Akeidah: Bincha — a child can be the product of kedusha, or it can be distorted by Giluy Arayos, which corrupts the power of creation. Yechidcha — this singular statement connects to Hashem, the One; Avodah Zarah is its opposite. Asher Ahavta — love, when distorted or unchecked, can lead to Shefichas Damim. Through Avraham's layered mesiras nefesh, we learn how to cleanse, uplift, and live with purpose.

Mesiras Nefesh Today: Personal Growth as Sacrifice

Today, we're not usually called to literal self-sacrifice. But we are called to stretch, to give, to grow. Giving tzedakah, our time, unique items, or things we are emotionally connected to — this too is mesiras nefesh. Letting go of something you have plenty of? That's one level. Giving something precious and unique? That's a deeper level. Offering up something you love? That's the ultimate. It's easy to speak of faith in the abstract, but the Akeidah teaches us to act on it in tangible ways. Bit by bit, sacrifice by sacrifice, we build ourselves into people who reflect our forefather Avraham. May we all have a Shabbos of warmth, reflection, and strength. And may our threes always point us upward.

Parshas Chayei Sarah

The Power of the Imahot: Nature, Nurture, and Rising Above

It's Not Just About the Fathers

In the last several weeks, we've been talking about zechut Avot — the power and impact of the fathers. But truth be told, it's not just all about the fathers. It's a husband, a wife, and Hashem together that make a child and bring this world into focus. The partnership of these three brings blessing, continuity, and purpose to the world. As we refocus on Parshas Chayei Sarah, we see zechut Imahot — the power and the zechut that we gain from the mothers. Their influence reverberates not only through our history, but in every Jewish home and every Jewish heart.

Chayei Sarah: A Life of Completion

At the very beginning of the parsha, we encounter remarkable words: 'And the life of Sarah was one hundred years and twenty years and seven years; the years of Sarah's life.' The way the verse is structured is unusual. Rashi explains that the Torah breaks down Sarah's age into separate segments to teach us something profound: at a hundred she was as free of sin as at twenty, and at twenty she was as beautiful as at seven. She lived a complete life — a life of shleimut.

There is a profound Chassidic teaching: when a person completes their tafkid in this world, when they've fulfilled the specific mitzvah for which they were created, their soul may return to its Source. Sarah's tafkid was Yitzchak. Not just to give birth to him, but to ensure he was brought up in such a way that he himself would have the strength and spiritual preparation to fulfill his role in the Akeidah. Consider this: he was 37 years old when the Akeidah happened. A 37-year-old intelligent man is not going to lie down on a sacrificial altar unless something profound was infused in him. That chinuch came in large part from his mother, Sarah.

Rivka: The Return of Sarah's Miracles

When Rivka entered Sarah's tent, something extraordinary happened. Rashi (Bereishis 24:67) explains that the miracles that had characterized Sarah's tent returned. The Midrash (Bereishis Rabbah 60:16) teaches that three miraculous signs accompanied Sarah's righteousness: the Shabbat candles she lit would burn from one Shabbat eve to the next; there was a blessing in her dough; and a cloud of glory hovered over her tent — a sign of the Divine Presence. These three miracles correspond to the three primary mitzvos associated with Jewish women: lighting Shabbat candles, separating challah, and maintaining family purity. Through these mitzvos, a Jewish woman creates a dwelling place for the Shechinah.

Nature versus Nurture: Breaking the Mold

Let us trace this theme through our forefathers. Adam HaRishon had no one to nurture him. Avraham Avinu — nurture would have dictated that he follow his father Terach into idol worship. His father manufactured and sold idols. Yet Avraham broke free entirely. He used his bechirah — his free will — to recognize truth and forge a new path. This teaches us that while nature and nurture may influence us profoundly, they do not determine our destiny.

We see this perhaps most dramatically in Rivka. She was raised by Betuel and Lavan — people characterized by deception, greed, and violence. Yet Rivka's personal awareness, even at a young age, told her clearly that this is a bad place to be and these are not the values she wants to live by. This is the gift of bechirah — the ability to transcend our circumstances. Have a wonderful, blessed Shabbat.

Parshas Toldos

Building Toldos with Awareness, Mesorah, and Responsibility

Parshas Toldos opens with a verse that at first glance seems simple, yet it contains a deep and powerful teaching about who we are and how we shape the future. The Torah says: 'Eileh toldos Yitzchak ben Avraham. Avraham holid es Yitzchak.' By introducing Yitzchak through Avraham, the Torah teaches that Toldos are not only about what emerges from me in the future, but also about the forces and people that shaped me from the past. Toldos is identity unfolding forward — a continuous path, where each step carries the awareness of what came before and the intention of what will come after. It is legacy.

Beginning with Creation: Toldos HaShamayim VehaAretz

To understand this deeply, we return to the first appearance of the word in the Torah. In Bereishis 2:4 the Torah states: 'Eileh toldos hashamayim veha'aretz b'hibaram' — 'These are the generations of the heavens and the earth when they were created.' This appears after creation is complete. HaShem embedded within reality the seeds of continuation. Even creation has Toldos, but unlike the first act of yesh meayin, the Toldos of creation unfold naturally, moving forward from what came before.

Toldos in Halacha: The Rambam's Definition

The Rambam, in his commentary to the Mishnah (Shabbos 7:2), defines a toladah as an act similar in result to one of the av melachos, but different in its method, intent, or manner. This halachic definition mirrors the Torah's idea of Toldos. Children do not replicate their parents. Students do not become identical to their teachers. Generations do not copy what came before. Instead, each generation continues the essence through new forms. The core stays the same. The vessel changes. Mesorah is not duplication. Mesorah is continuation.

Avraham, Yitzchak, and the Conscious Choice to Create Toldos

People often say that any man can be a father, but it takes a man to be a dad. In the Torah, to be holid means purposeful involvement. It means choosing to build something that will outlive me. Avraham holid es Yitzchak. Avraham shaped Yitzchak with presence and intention. Yitzchak, known for his gevurah, held himself with discipline and clarity. He partnered with Rivka, established a home of purpose, and continued Avraham's mission with HaShem as the third partner. Toldos does not happen by accident. Toldos is created with kavvanah and intention.

The Balance of Yaakov: Tiferes Gives Birth to Greatness

Kabbalah teaches that Avraham is chesed, Yitzchak is gevurah, and Yaakov is tiferes — the harmonious balance between the two. Because Yaakov embodies this balance, he expands beyond both of them. His children become the Shevatim. Before building his home, Yaakov immerses himself in the yeshiva of Shem and Ever. Chazal explain that he paused to strengthen his mesorah before building the future. He asks the essential question of Toldos: to know who I must become, I must first know where I come from.

The Midrash on Toldos: Fruits of the Tzaddikim

Bereishis Rabbah comments on the toldos of Noach with the teaching: 'Ikar toldoseihem shel tzaddikim — ma'asim tovim' — 'The primary offspring of the righteous are their good deeds.' Our Toldos are not only our children. They are our maasim, our dibburim, our machshavos, and our middos. The Maharal explains that every mitzvah performed through machshavah, dibbur, and maaseh creates spiritual Toldos that ascend through all the worlds. May we merit to build generations of goodness, actions that ripple forward, and Toldos that carry the mission of our Avos into the future. A beautiful Shabbos.

Parshas Vayetzei

When Speech Builds and Listening Unites

Foundational Themes

Parshas Vayetzei is a parsha of transition. The Torah opens, 'Vayetzei Yaakov miBe'er Sheva vayelech Charanah' (Bereishis 28:10) — Yaakov leaves Be'er Sheva and walks toward Charan, a movement not only of place but of identity. Yaakov Avinu leaves his parents' home, leaves safety, and steps into exile. This is where the Jewish people are first formed — not in holiness, not in comfort, but inside complexity. At the heart of the parsha stands a defining theme: the balance of speaking and listening, and the power of letters and words to either fracture or unify. This is not merely communication, it is relationship.

Leaving and Being Felt

When Yaakov leaves Be'er Sheva, Chazal teach that the city feels his absence. There is a difference between someone whose departure brings relief and someone whose departure leaves emptiness. Yaakov belonged to the latter. The Torah teaches us something powerful here: it is not only who you are when you arrive that matters — it is who you are when you leave.

The Stones and the Letters

The Torah says, 'Vayikach me'avnei hamakom' (Bereishis 28:11) — he took from the stones of the place. Rashi describes the scene beautifully: the stones began arguing with one another, each one saying, 'Let the righteous one rest his head upon me.' Immediately, Hashem made them into one stone — turning rivalry into unity. Chassidus deepens this idea. The Alter Rebbe brings a teaching from Sefer Yetzirah: two letters build two words, three letters build six words, four letters build twenty-four words. Letters do not merely add meaning — they multiply it. But Yaakov's stones move in the opposite direction: not from one to many, but from many to one. Words can build worlds, but they can also fracture them. When speech is fragmented, relationships crumble. When speech is unified, holiness enters.

Three Styles of Speech

Avraham, from chesed, spoke outward — he challenged the world, argued with Hashem for good things, brought strangers into his tent. Yitzchak, gevurah, spoke inward — he was formed through silence; his tefillah is private, he accepts reality. And Yaakov? He was tiferes — beauty and balance. He speaks between people. He negotiates, explains, listens. And the result is that he creates real relationships through conversation.

The Art of Listening

Yaakov's greatness is not only in how he speaks, but in how he listens. He listens to Rivkah when she tells him to take the brachah (Bereishis 27:8-10). He listens to Rachel and Leah before leaving Lavan (Bereishis 31:4-16). He listens to Yosef's dreams and 'aviv shamar et hadavar' (Bereishis 37:11) — he guarded the matter. And standing before Pharaoh — the most powerful man on earth — when asked 'How many are the days of your life?', Yaakov gives no performance. He answers from truth: 'Me'at vera'im hayu yemei shnei chayai' — 'My life was hard. Few were my days. I did not reach my fathers.' That is a man who has listened to his own story.

Closing Thought

Avraham changed the world with speech. Yitzchak deepened the soul with silence. Yaakov built a nation through conversation. He teaches that holiness does not live in volume or withdrawal. It lives in relationship — listening with intention, speaking with care, and answering with honesty. Shabbos invites us into what Yaakov mastered. We turn off the noise, we put down distance, and we undo fracture. We speak, listen, and then we reconnect. Not as performers. Not as commentators. As people. As family. As Jews. Many letters can build many worlds. But unity builds eternity.

Parshas Vayishlach

Standing in Front

The Meaning of Vayishlach: Sending Forward

The word Vayishlach means 'and he sent out.' The Torah opens with this word (Bereishis 32:4): 'Vayishlach Yaakov malachim lefanav el Esav achiv' — And Yaakov sent messengers ahead of him to Eisav his brother. But there is a deeper question here: Why now? Why is Yaakov ready to face Eisav at this particular moment?

The Prerequisite: Yosef's Birth

If you look at last week's parsha, when Yaakov prepares to leave Lavan, the Torah tells us: 'Vayehi ka'asher yaldah Rachel et Yosef' — And it was when Rachel gave birth to Yosef. Rashi explains that it wasn't until Yosef was born that Yaakov was ready to leave and eventually face Eisav. Why? Because Yosef was the only one who would have the koach to take on Eisav. The Midrash (Bereishis Rabbah 73:7) teaches that Yosef is compared to fire, while Eisav is compared to straw.

The Three-Pronged Approach

Yaakov's response to the threat is methodical and comprehensive. The mefarshim teach that Yaakov prepared himself in three ways: bedor on, b'tefillah, uv'milchamah — with gifts, with prayer, and with war. The Torah describes each preparation: the gifts sent in waves to appease Eisav; the prayer where Yaakov calls out, 'Hatzileini na miyad achi miyad Eisav ki yare anochi oso' — Save me please from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Eisav; and the preparation for war, dividing his camp so that at least some would survive.

Wrestling with the Angel: A Test of Strength

A man wrestles with Yaakov all night long. The Torah describes (Bereishis 32:25-26): 'Vaya'avek ish imo ad alot hashachar. Vayar ki lo yachol lo' — And a man wrestled with him until the break of dawn. And when he saw that he could not prevail against him. Rashi explains that this 'man' was the ministering angel of Eisav — the spiritual force behind Eisav's physical power. The wrestling match wasn't just physical; it was spiritual warfare. And Yaakov prevailed. The angel then changes his name (Bereishis 32:29): 'Lo Yaakov ye'amer od shimcha ki im Yisrael ki sarita im Elokim v'im anashim vatuchal' — No longer will your name be called Yaakov, but Yisrael, for you have struggled with the divine and with men, and you have prevailed. This is the moment of transformation.

Standing in Front: The Ultimate Leadership

And now comes the moment of truth. When Yaakov finally meets his brother, the Torah tells us (Bereishis 33:3): 'V'hu avar lifneihem' — And he passed before them. Yaakov doesn't hide behind his wives. He doesn't hide behind his children. He stands in front. It's no longer a situation of vayishlach — sending someone else forward. The time for preparation is over. Now is the time for action, for leadership, for standing at the head. This is not just a level of mesiras nefesh. He's ready to stand and fight. The head, the rosh, the leader, knows they are supposed to be at the head.

The Lesson for Our Lives

Yaakov teaches us that true leadership isn't about being the strongest or the loudest. It's about knowing when to gather information and when to act. It's about standing in front when it matters most — protecting what we hold dear by placing ourselves at risk. It's about the courage to face our fears, to wrestle with our challenges, and to emerge transformed, ready to stand at the head. May we all merit to know when to prepare and when to act, when to send others forward and when to go forward ourselves. May we have the wisdom to distinguish between harm that builds and danger that destroys. And may we always have the courage to stand in front when it truly matters. Have a wonderful Shabbos.
